title: The Hut Outside the Town
summary: Kāṇha, a kāpālika yogi, sings to Ḍombī, the untouchable woman whose hut stands outside the town. A shaven brahmin goes by touching, she dances on a lotus of sixty-four petals and comes and goes in someone's boat, he puts on a garland of bones for her, and she breaks the lake and eats the lotus root, and he vows to kill her. Munidatta reads Ḍombī as Nairātmā (selflessness as a goddess) and the purified central channel, her hut as the wheel of great bliss and the lotus as the wheel of emanation; in the last couplet, for one without the guru's lineage, she is the unpurified channel, and killing her means making her without inherent nature.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heading reads de sha kha zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyis so, 'the melody called Deśākha, by Kṛṣṇācārya' (nag po spyod pa'i zhabs). It confirms the name of the rāga and adds the poet, whom the Bengali heading does not name. The translation follows the Bengali; see questions.
Printed bārihirem̐, for the expected bāhire(m̐) 'outside' (locative). Transliterated as printed. The sense is not in doubt, and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has phyi rol 'outside'.

lines.translit: chaichoi jāi so bāhma nāṛiā || dhru ||
lines.gloss: touching-touching · goes · that · brahmin · shaven-headed (or: lad?) · (refrain cue)
lines.en: Touching and touching, that shaven-headed [brahmin]{brahmin} goes by.

flags.note: chaichoi: chosen 'touching again and again'. Munidatta renders it spṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā (cp.10.m2) and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has reg gin reg gin, 'touching, touching', so both old readings take it as repeated touching. The alternative 'barely touching, brushing past', which would picture the brahmin avoiding contact, has no support from either. The object (the hut? Ḍombī?) is unstated in the source and left unstated here.

nāṛiā: taken as 'shaven-headed' (compare Bengali nāṛā, nẽṛā 'shaven, bald'), as in the glossary entry for brahmin. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bram ze'i bu, 'brahmin's son, brahmin boy', for bāhma nāṛiā. That takes nāṛiā as 'lad', or follows Munidatta's gloss cittavaṭuka, 'mind-lad', which the Tibetan of the commentary renders sems ni bram ze'i bu (cp.10.m2). A young brahmin student wears the tonsure, so the two senses meet. Alternative English: 'that brahmin boy'.

Divergence: in the song the verb jāi is third person with 'that brahmin' as subject, and the Tibetan translation of the verse agrees ('gro de bram ze'i bu, 'goes that brahmin boy'). Munidatta's paraphrase has 'you go, touching and touching' (gacchasi), followed by 'O Nairātmā', so in his gloss the one who touches and goes appears to be Ḍombī. The Tibetan of the commentary keeps his second person (khyod 'gro) (cp.10.m2). Translated as the song stands, not harmonized.
The refrain cue ধ্রু already stands after this first couplet, not only after the refrain and later couplets. Not translated. See questions.

lines.translit: ālo ḍombi toe sama karibe ma sāṅga
lines.gloss: hey · Ḍombī · you-with · with · will-make · by-me · company
lines.en: Hey [Ḍombī]{dombi}, I will keep company with you;

flags.note: sāṅga (Sanskrit saṅga): 'company, association, attachment', and also sexual union. 'Keep company with' is chosen because it carries both the social and the erotic sense. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mnyam 'grogs bya, 'I will keep company with you', which supports it. Munidatta paraphrases with abhiṣvaṅga, 'close attachment, embrace' (cp.10.m3), which the Tibetan of the commentary renders mngon par 'khyud pa, 'embrace'.

lines.translit: nighiṇa kāhna kāpāli joi lāga || dhru ||
lines.gloss: without-disgust · Kāṇha · kāpālika · yogi · attached(?) · (refrain cue)

flags.note: lāga: taken as 'clings, is attached' (Old Bengali lāg- 'stick to'). This fits Munidatta's 'holding [you] constantly, without interval' (cp.10.m3). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no word for it: kAh+Na thod pa'i rnal 'byor skyug bro spangs, 'Kāhna, the skull yogi who has given up revulsion', is a verbless description of the speaker. So the Tibetan gives no evidence for lāga, and its source may have lacked the word. Alternatives: 'for (your sake)', compare lāgi; or, if the text were lāṅga (which would rhyme with sāṅga), 'naked'. That last one is only my conjecture. 'close' is added so that the English verb can stand without an object.

The printed ekaso is read as eka so, 'that one', answered by tahim̐ 'on it' in 3b. Munidatta's lemma is 'eka so' (cp.10.m4), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gcig nyid, 'the one alone, that very one'. 'A single' renders eka so.

lines.translit: tahim̐ caṛi nācaa ḍombī bāpuṛī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: on-it · having-climbed · dances · Ḍombī · poor/wretched · (refrain cue)

flags.note: bāpuṛī: 'poor, wretched, lowly'. It could express pity, affection or contempt; 'poor' is chosen as the most open. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) seems to transliterate the word rather than translate it (gar byed pa pu lI'i, where pa pu lI appears to stand for bāpuṛī), and Munidatta does not gloss it, so neither witness helps with its sense.

Divergence: in the song Ḍombī climbs the lotus and dances, and the Tibetan translation of the verse agrees (g.yung mo gar byed, 'the low-caste woman dances'). Munidatta has Kṛṣṇācārya dancing there together with Nairātmā (cp.10.m4). Not harmonized.

caṛi 'climbing (onto)': the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has der gnas, 'staying there', which matches Munidatta's paraphrase tatra sthitvā (cp.10.m4) rather than the verb of the song. The Bengali caṛ- 'climb, mount' is clear, and the translation keeps it.

lines.en: Hey [Ḍombī]{dombi}, I ask you in good faith:

flags.note: The opening words are unstable across the witnesses. The song has hālo ḍombī. Munidatta's lemma is 'hañcū lo' (cp.10.m5), which the Tibetan of the commentary renders kye'i khyod, 'O you'. The Tibetan translation of the verse has no vocative at all and begins bdag gis g.yung mo khyod la, 'I … you, low-caste woman'. Munidatta's text, and the Tibetan translators', may have read differently here. The translation follows the song.

sadabhāve (Sanskrit sadbhāva): 'in good faith, sincerely', the usual sense, is chosen. The word also means 'true being, reality'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders it bden dngos, literally 'true thing', and Munidatta explains it as 'with an intention set on the true nature' (svarūpāśayena, cp.10.m5), so both lean toward the second sense; the Tibetan line could mean 'I asked you about the truth'. The Tibetan also has the past dris 'asked' for the present puchami.

lines.translit: aisasi jāsi ḍombi kāhari nāvem̐ || dhru ||
lines.gloss: you-come · you-go · Ḍombī · whose · in/by-boat · (refrain cue)
lines.en: in whose [boat]{boat} do you come and go, [Ḍombī]{dombi}?

lines.translit: tānti vikaṇaa ḍombī avara nā caṅgatā
lines.gloss: cord/string · sells · Ḍombī · more/other · not · basket(?)

flags.note: avara nā caṅgatā is unclear. I chose avara 'more, other' + nā 'not' + caṅgatā 'basket(s)'. That gives 'and no more baskets', which leaves open both 'no longer' and 'no other'. Alternatives: (1) Munidatta treats the cord and the cāṅgita as two things she 'sells', that is, gives up (cp.10.m6), and the Tibetan translation does the same (see the witness flag). That suggests 'cord, and baskets too', with nā corrupt or not a negative. (2) Read caṅgatā as caṅga-tā 'goodness, excellence': 'Ḍombī sells cord; she has nothing else of worth'. (3) Read avaranā as āvaraṇa 'covering, mat': 'cord, mats and baskets'. The sense 'basket' for caṅgatā is a guess (compare later Bengali cāṅāri, a flat bamboo basket); the Tibetan's 'flower-stand' gives it some support.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rgyud 'tshong g.yung mo gzhan yang me tog stegs, 'the low-caste woman sells cord, and also a flower-stand (or flower-tray)'. It has no negative for nā, takes avara as 'and also' (gzhan yang), and renders caṅgatā as me tog stegs, literally 'flower platform', the same words its commentary uses for Munidatta's cāṅgita (cp.10.m6). With Munidatta, then, it has two things sold. The line translates the Bengali as printed, with its negative; the Tibetan puts that reading in doubt.

tānti: 'cord', following Munidatta's tantrī 'string, cord' (cp.10.m6). The Tibetan translation has rgyud for both, a word that means 'string, thread' as well as 'tantra' and 'lineage', so it does not narrow the sense. An instrument string, thread, or a loom (Bengali tā̃t) are also possible.

vikaṇaa is a third-person form ('Ḍombī sells'), and the Tibetan translation of the verse keeps the third person (rgyud 'tshong g.yung mo, 'the low-caste woman sells cord'). Munidatta renders it in the second person with 'O Ḍombī' (cp.10.m6), and ḍombī could be a vocative here. The third person is kept.

lines.gloss: your · for-the-sake-of · having-left + performer's/reed(?) · basket/box(?) · (refrain cue)
lines.en: for your sake I have given up the performer's basket.

flags.note: chāṛinaṛa eṭṭā is obscure. I read it as chāṛi naṛa (p)eṭṭā, 'left the performer's basket', guided by Munidatta's 'like an actor (naṭavat) I have abandoned the basket (peṭaka) of saṃsāra' (cp.10.m6). Reading naṛa as naṭa (Prakrit naḍa) follows him; the missing p of peṭṭā is my assumption. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads the line differently: khyod kyi ched du 'dam bu'i stan gzhag go, 'for your sake a seat (or mat) of reeds is laid down'. It takes naṛa as naḍa 'reed' ('dam bu), has 'seat, mat' (stan) where the Bengali has eṭṭā, and 'set down' (gzhag, which can also mean 'leave') for chāṛi. Its commentary, however, follows Munidatta (gar mkhan bzhin du 'like a dancer', 'khor ba'i mdzod 'the chest of saṃsāra', cp.10.m6), so the Tibetan verse and commentary disagree. Other alternatives: 'the reed basket' (naṛa 'reed' with Munidatta's basket), or eṭṭā = 'this'. See questions.

No subject is expressed, in the Bengali or in the Tibetan. 'I' is supplied from the parallel line 6b (moe 'by me') and from Munidatta's mayā (cp.10.m6). tohora antare is rendered 'for your sake', like Munidatta's tavāntareṇa. The Tibetan translation has khyod kyi ched du, 'for your sake', here and in 6b, which supports this against 'because of you'.

lines.gloss: you · (vocative particle to a woman) · Ḍombī · I · kāpālika

flags.note: ḍombī is taken as a vocative, with tu lo 'you there' as the call. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has kye khyod g.yung mo bdag ni ka pA li; kye khyod 'O you' is the usual Tibetan form of address, and Munidatta too has 'O Ḍombī' (bho ḍomvi, cp.10.m7). lo, a familiar particle used to a woman, is rendered 'Hey', as the Tibetan renders it kye. The Bengali also allows two verbless clauses, 'you are a Ḍombī; I am a kāpālika', which sets the two outcastes side by side.

lines.translit: tohora antare moe ghalili hāṛeri mālī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: your · for-the-sake-of · by-me · put-on · of-bone · garland · (refrain cue)
lines.en: For your sake I have put on a [garland of bones]{bone-garland}.

flags.note: bhāñjīa 'having broken' could mean breaking up the water or breaching the bank. The song does not say which, and the Tibetan translation's bcom nas, 'having smashed, destroyed', does not decide it. It is rendered plainly as 'Breaking'.

lines.en: I will kill [Ḍombī]{dombi}; I will take her life.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads g.yung mo blangs nas bdag gi pha rol gsod, 'having taken the low-caste woman, I kill the other (or: my adversary)'. It makes Ḍombī the object of lemi 'I take' rather than of mārami 'I kill', and reads parāṇa as para 'other' (pha rol) rather than prāṇa 'life'. In the Tibetan, then, the poet takes Ḍombī and kills someone else. The Bengali parāṇa is the ordinary vernacular form of prāṇa 'life', and the translation follows it, but the Tibetan puts the sense of the line in doubt. Munidatta explains 'I kill' as 'I make without inherent nature' without naming the object explicitly (cp.10.m8).

mārami and lemi are first-person present forms, which Old Bengali also uses for the future; 'will' is chosen because the line is a threat. 'her' is supplied in 'her life'. ḍombī could also be a vocative: 'I will kill you, Ḍombī; I will take your life'.

notes.text: The Bengali heading names only the rāga. The ascription to Kāṇha rests on the song itself, where he names himself in couplet 2, and on Munidatta, who introduces the song as spoken by Kṛṣṇapāda, Kāṇha's Sanskrit name (cp.10.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) names the poet in its heading: de sha kha zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyis so, 'the melody called Deśākha, by Kṛṣṇācārya' (nag po spyod pa is the Tibetan form of his name).

Structure: the poet names himself in couplet 2, which the input marks as the refrain, and not in the last couplet. Shastri prints the refrain cue ধ্রু after 1b as well as after 2b and every later couplet; it is not translated. Munidatta numbers his divisions so that couplet 3 is 'the second pada' and couplets 4 to 7 are the third to the sixth (cp.10.m4, cp.10.m5, cp.10.m6, cp.10.m7, cp.10.m8).

Throughout the song the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders ḍombī with the common noun g.yung mo, 'low-caste woman', instead of transliterating it, and its commentary does the same: Munidatta's 'the word Ḍombī' (ḍombīśabda) becomes g.yung mo'i sgra (cp.10.m1). The translators read the word as the name of a caste rather than of a person.
Munidatta introduces the song as Kṛṣṇapāda telling 'that same matter', through his realization of the nature of selflessness, 'in the twilight language of the word Ḍombī' (cp.10.m1).

The Tibetan translation renders Munidatta's sandhyābhāṣā, 'twilight language', as dgongs pa'i skad, 'language of intention' (cp.10.m1), which bears on the old question whether sandhyā, 'twilight', or sandhā, 'intention', is meant. It also renders his 'that same matter' (tam evārthaṃ) as de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of suchness'.
Rāga: a melodic mode. The heading names the mode to which the song is sung, Deśākha. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders rāga as glu dbyangs, 'melody', and spells the name de sha kha.
The Ḍoms were treated as untouchable and made to live at the edge of settlements. A Ḍom woman's hut outside the town is ordinary social geography before it is anything else.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads grong khyer phyi rol g.yung mo khyod kyi khyim, 'outside the town, low-caste woman, your house'. It agrees with the Bengali, but its khyim is 'house, home' rather than a word for a hut. That matches Munidatta's tavāgāra, 'your house', which the Tibetan of the commentary also renders khyod kyi khyim (cp.10.m2). The translation keeps the Bengali kuṛiā, 'hut'.

Munidatta says she is called Ḍombī because she cannot be touched, and is to be understood as the purified avadhūtī (the central channel of the subtle body), Nairātmā (selflessness personified as a goddess). The town is the mass of sense objects, beginning with visible form. Outside it, beyond the range of the senses, is 'your house', the wheel of great bliss. He, the siddha master (an accomplished adept) Kṛṣṇapāda, came to know it through the guru's lineage (cp.10.m2).

Where Munidatta speaks of the bodhicitta 'of yogins who lack the lineage' (asampradāyayogināṃ), the Tibetan translation of his comment has the opposite: man ngag thob pa'i rnal 'byor pas, 'by the yogin who has obtained the instruction'. It has no negative (cp.10.m2).

chaichoi is a reduplicated form of the verb 'touch'. Munidatta renders it spṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā, 'touching and touching' (cp.10.m2). nāṛiā is taken as 'shaven', the tonsure of a young brahmin student; Munidatta calls him a vaṭuka, a boy of that kind (cp.10.m2). The transliteration gives jāi for the machine's yāi, since the verb is jā- 'go' (compare jāsi in 4b); the Tibetan has 'gro, 'goes'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads reg gin reg gin 'gro de bram ze'i bu, 'touching, touching, goes that brahmin boy'. Its bram ze'i bu, 'brahmin's son, brahmin boy', takes nāṛiā as 'lad' rather than 'shaven-headed', in line with Munidatta's cittavaṭuka, 'mind-lad', which the Tibetan of the commentary renders sems ni bram ze'i bu, 'the mind is the brahmin boy' (cp.10.m2). In the verse the Tibetan keeps the song's third person; in the commentary it keeps Munidatta's 'you go' (khyod 'gro).
A brahmin's purity rules forbid contact with a Ḍom. The line puts one at the edge of her world, touching. The song does not say what he touches.

Munidatta reads the brahmin as the 'mind-lad' (cittavaṭuka). It is born from the seed syllable HŪṂ, which he calls brahma, and it is a lad because the mind is fickle. His paraphrase then turns to the second person: '[you] go, touching and touching, from the jewel-root, the joy of cessation, the bodhicitta (mind of awakening) of yogins who lack the lineage, which in conventional terms has the form of semen. O Nairātmā.' In his gloss the one who touches and goes therefore seems to be Ḍombī herself (cp.10.m2). The Tibetan translation of the comment speaks instead of the yogin who has obtained the instruction; see the witness note on couplet 1.

sāṅga (Sanskrit saṅga) means company, association or attachment, and can mean sexual union. Munidatta paraphrases: 'I must make close attachment (abhiṣvaṅga) with you' (cp.10.m3). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of the line reads kye'i g.yung mo khyod dang mnyam 'grogs bya, 'O low-caste woman, I will keep company with you'; its commentary renders abhiṣvaṅga as mngon par 'khyud pa, 'embrace'.

kāpāli: a kāpālika, an ascetic who carries a skull-bowl, wears bone ornaments and disregards caste purity. nighiṇa (Sanskrit nirghṛṇa) means 'without disgust'; Munidatta adds 'free of faults such as shame' (cp.10.m3). lāga is taken as 'attached, clinging'; see the flag on the line.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads kAh+Na thod pa'i rnal 'byor skyug bro spangs, 'Kāhna, the skull yogi who has given up revulsion'. It transliterates the vernacular name (Kāhna), where its heading and commentary use the Tibetan name nag po spyod pa. It takes kāpāli as qualifying joi, 'skull yogi', as the English does. It renders nighiṇa analytically, 'having given up revulsion' (skyug bro spangs). And it has no word for lāga.

Munidatta has Kāṇha say: 'As my nature is, so I am', without disgust. Holding [her] constantly and without interval, he gains the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā (the 'Great Seal', the highest attainment), whose nature is wisdom and means. He cites the Hevajra: 'Hear from me the tantra whose nature is wisdom and means' (cp.10.m3).

For Munidatta's 'as my nature is, so I am' (yādṛśasvabhāvas tādṛśo), the Tibetan translation of the comment has gang dang 'dra ba'i gnas de dang 'dra ba dag la, 'in places of whatever kind', as if reading 'place' for 'nature': whatever the place, he is free of revulsion and shame (cp.10.m3).

Munidatta calls this couplet 'the place of practice'. The one lotus is the wheel of emanation, which has sixty-four petals. There Kṛṣṇācārya, lovely with the joy of great passion, dances in one taste with the Blessed Lady Nairātmā. He cites the Hevajra: 'Dance in the form of Heruka' (cp.10.m4). In the song the dancer is Ḍombī.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads gcig nyid pad 'dab drug cu rtsa bzhi la / der gnas g.yung mo gar byed pa pu lI'i, roughly 'on the one lotus of sixty-four petals, staying there, the low-caste woman dances …'. It renders eka so as gcig nyid, 'the one alone', and compresses lotus and petals into pad 'dab. For caṛi, 'climbing', it has der gnas, 'staying there', which matches Munidatta's tatra sthitvā (cp.10.m4). pa pu lI'i seems to transliterate bāpuṛī rather than translate it. Like the song, and unlike Munidatta, it makes the woman the dancer.

Munidatta says this couplet makes the realization of selflessness firm. He paraphrases: 'O Nairātmā, I ask you in good faith, that is, intent on your own nature: by whose path, the boat of conventional bodhicitta, do you come and go?' He gives the meaning as 'you do not', because everything consists of the innate. He then cites the Hevajra: the whole world is innate, the innate is called one's own nature, and one's own nature is nirvāṇa to a mind of pure form (cp.10.m5).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads bdag gis g.yung mo khyod la bden dngos dris / 'ong dang 'gro ba gang gi gru la byed, 'I asked you, low-caste woman, about the truth (or: truly): in whose boat do you come and go?' It has no vocative for hālo, renders sadabhāve as bden dngos, literally 'true thing', and leaves out the name in 4b. Its commentary's lemma is kye'i khyod, 'O you', where Munidatta's printed lemma is hañcū lo, and it renders svarūpāśayena as bden pa'i dngos po'i rang bzhin gyi bsam pas, 'with an intention on the nature of the true thing' (cp.10.m5).
A river boat, crossing and recrossing. Kāṇha asks whose boat carries her to and fro, and the song does not answer.

The couplet is the hardest in the song. For tānti, caṅgatā, avara nā and chāṛinaṛa eṭṭā see the flags on 5a and 5b. Munidatta's lemma cāṅgita differs from the song's caṅgatā (cp.10.m6). He also has the 'basket' (peṭaka) and the 'actor' (naṭa) that 5b seems to contain (cp.10.m6).

Munidatta says this couplet states the true nature of selflessness. He takes tānti as tantrī and reads it as the bhaga (the female organ), 'the place of the lotus', which has the form of ignorance. The cāṅgita is its offshoot, the appearance of objects. Addressing Ḍombī as Nairātmā, he says that by the grace of the guru's feet she makes for him the selling, that is the giving up, of these two. And so, like an actor, he has abandoned the basket of saṃsāra for her sake (cp.10.m6).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rgyud 'tshong g.yung mo gzhan yang me tog stegs, 'the low-caste woman sells cord, and also a flower-stand'. It has no negative corresponding to nā. It takes avara as 'and also' (gzhan yang). For caṅgatā it has me tog stegs, literally 'flower platform', perhaps a tray or stand for flowers, the same words its commentary uses for Munidatta's cāṅgita (cp.10.m6). Like Munidatta, then, it has two things sold. rgyud, which renders both tānti and Munidatta's tantrī, also means 'tantra' and 'lineage'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads khyod kyi ched du 'dam bu'i stan gzhag go, 'for your sake a seat (or mat) of reeds is laid down'. It takes naṛa as naḍa, 'reed' ('dam bu), has 'seat, mat' (stan) where the Bengali has eṭṭā, and 'set down' (gzhag, which can also mean 'leave') for chāṛi. Its translation of the commentary, however, follows Munidatta's actor and basket: gar mkhan bzhin du, 'like a dancer', and 'khor ba'i mdzod, 'the chest (or store) of saṃsāra' (cp.10.m6).

In the Tibetan translation of Munidatta's comment the thing to be given up is the selling of oneself, bdag nyid 'tshong ba, where the printed Sanskrit has mama vikrayaṇaṃ, 'the selling … for me' (Shastri marks a variant at this point). And 'you make' becomes a command: khyod kyis yongs su spong bar byos, 'you must give it up' (cp.10.m6).

Munidatta says this couplet describes the lord of yogis' conduct 'with elaboration'. Kāṇha knows Ḍombī, Nairātmā, in her own nature through the true guru's grace. He is a kāpālika and a bearer of conduct, and Munidatta explains the word as one able to protect (pāl-) 'ka', her bliss, a play on the syllables. For her sake Kṛṣṇācārya took up conduct with the wheel, earrings, necklace and other ornaments, which the gloss links with the six tathāgatas (buddhas who head the tantric families). Not relying on outer mantras and tantras, he sported with the five colours (pañcavarṇa). The qualifier niraṃśu in that compound is unclear to me; the Tibetan translation has bone ornaments at this point, as the witness note on the couplet explains (cp.10.m7).

Munidatta supports this with an Apabhraṃśa verse by Kṛṣṇācārya. Roughly: not one mantra, not one tantra is to be done; taking one's own housewife one makes love; as long as the housewife is not immersed in one's own house, how can one sport in the five colours? The verse is terse and this rendering is tentative (cp.10.m7).

The Tibetan translation of Munidatta's comment differs from the printed Sanskrit in three places. Among the ornaments of conduct it lists bone ornaments ('the wheel of the six tathāgatas, earrings, necklace and bone ornaments', rus rgyan), where the Sanskrit has the unclear niraṃśu. For 'sporting with the five colours' (pañcavarṇaviharaṇa) it has rigs lnga'i spyod lam, 'the conduct of the five families', taking varṇa in its other sense, 'class, caste'. In Kṛṣṇācārya's verse it has ma dag pa, 'not purified', for ṇa majjai. It also spells out the syllable play: kaM ni khyod kyi bde ba, pA ni skyong bar nus pa, 'kaṃ is your bliss; pā is being able to protect it' (cp.10.m7).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads kye khyod g.yung mo bdag ni ka pA li, 'O you, low-caste woman, I am a kāpālika'. kye khyod is the usual Tibetan form of address, so the Tibetan, like Munidatta (bho ḍomvi, cp.10.m7), takes ḍombī as a vocative; it renders the particle lo as kye. It transliterates kapālī (ka pA li), where in 2b it translated kāpāli as thod pa'i, 'skull-'.

A garland of bone beads or carved bone belongs to a kāpālika's regalia; the poet takes it on for Ḍombī's sake. Munidatta's gloss on the couplet speaks of the ornaments of tantric conduct but does not name the garland; the Tibetan translation of the gloss includes bone ornaments (rus rgyan) among them (cp.10.m7).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees with the Bengali: khyod kyi ched du bdag gi rus phreng bcas, 'for your sake I have put on a bone garland'. Its phreng ba can mean a rosary as well as a garland.
Lotus roots grow in the mud of pond beds and are dug up for food. 'Breaking' the lake may mean breaking up its surface or breaching its banks to get at them.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees: rdzing bu bcom nas g.yung mo pad rtsa zos, 'having smashed the pond, the low-caste woman ate the lotus root'. rdzing bu is 'pond, pool', the word its commentary uses for sarovara, and in lus kyi rdzing bu, 'the pool of the body', for Munidatta's kāyapuṣkara (cp.10.m8). pad rtsa, 'lotus root', confirms the sense of molāṇa.

Munidatta says the last couplet states that Ḍombinī is of two kinds. For one who lacks the guru's lineage, this same Ḍombī is the unpurified avadhūtī. The lake is the body as a lotus pool (kāyapuṣkara), and its root is bodhicitta, which in conventional terms has the form of semen. He explains 'I kill' as 'I make without inherent nature' (cp.10.m8).

Munidatta closes with a Prakrit verse from what he calls vahiśāstra, 'an outside treatise'; the Tibetan translation has phyi rol gyi bstan bcos, 'an outer treatise'. As printed the Prakrit is corrupt, but it seems to say that the same water becomes poison in a snake's mouth and pearls in an oyster shell, which would illustrate Ḍombī's two kinds. The Tibetan version supports this: water blessed by mantra gains honour according to its vessel; swallowed into a snake's mouth …; spat out by an oyster, pearl (cp.10.m8).
parāṇa (Sanskrit prāṇa) means 'breath, life'; it is the ordinary vernacular form of the word. The song gives no reason for the threat.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads g.yung mo blangs nas bdag gi pha rol gsod, 'having taken the low-caste woman, I kill the other (or: my adversary)'. It makes Ḍombī the object of 'take' (lemi, blangs nas) and reads parāṇa as para, 'other' (pha rol), not prāṇa, 'life'. In the Tibetan, then, the poet takes the woman and kills someone else. Its commentary, like Munidatta's, explains the killing as making without inherent nature (rang bzhin med par byed pa, cp.10.m8).
